## 2

I understand why it’s tempting to doubt large institutions—there are plenty of times throughout history when governments and official narratives haven't been honest. 

Where the flat Earth idea falls apart for me, though, isn't about trusting NASA or satellite imagery. It’s that you don't need space photos to observe curvature; humans figured this out thousands of years ago with simple geometry. If the Earth were flat, lunar eclipses wouldn't consistently cast a round shadow, cargo ships wouldn't disappear bottom-first over the horizon, and you wouldn't see entirely different constellations as you travel south of the equator. 

Beyond that, keeping something like this a secret would require literally millions of commercial pilots, navigators, surveyors, and rival governments who hate each other to maintain the exact same lie for generations without a single leak. The simpler, physically consistent explanation is just that the world is a sphere.

## 3

Think of sunlight as looking white, but actually containing every color of the rainbow mixed together. 

Light travels in waves, and different colors have different wave sizes. Red light travels in long, lazy waves, while blue light travels in short, choppy, energetic waves.

When sunlight hits Earth, it has to pass through our atmosphere, which is packed full of tiny gas molecules—mostly nitrogen and oxygen. The long, lazy red and yellow waves pass right through those molecules without bumping into them much. But the short, choppy blue waves are almost the exact same size as the gas particles, so they run straight into them and bounce off in every possible direction. 

This bouncing is called *scattering*. When you look up during the day, you aren't seeing light beamed straight from the Sun; you're seeing all that scattered blue light bouncing off the air above you and into your eyes. 

(And here's a bonus: at sunset, the light has to travel through way more air to reach you, so all the blue light scatters away before it gets to your eyes—leaving only the reds and oranges.)
